newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians give UDF strong mandate for reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians give UDF strong mandate for reform.

text.p: With almost all the results counted from Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the reformist Union of Democratic Forces and its allies were headed on Sunday for a comfortable win.
The UDF won 52 percent of the votes cast.
Their victory seals the rejection of the ex-communist Socialists in Bulgaria, a process begun with the election of President Petar Stoyanov on the UDF ticket in November.
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), toppled in February by UDF-led mass protests, had controlled almost all of Bulgaria's nine governments since the end of one-party rule in 1989.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov said the new government's four main priorities would be carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files of public figures, and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.
With just over 90 percent of the vote counted, the Socialists had 22 percent of the vote and three smaller parties were also set to enter parliament.
"The Blues alone at the top for the first time, record fall for the BSP" read a headline in Troud daily, while Standard said "Grand blue victory, the UDF will have 149 deputies".
Stoyanov indicated on Saturday night that he expected the UDF parliamentary group to nominate Kostov as prime minister.
"In every country after a decisive victory of a certain political force its leader becomes prime minister," he said.
The turnout, put at 58.31 percent, was the lowest for any election since the end of one-party rule in 1989, but the results of Saturday's poll had been seen as almost a foregone conclusion.

"We will be a constructive opposition and will continue to represent the ideas of reason and agreement, especially when it comes to the structural reform and financial stabilisation of the country," Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov told reporters.

A restrictive fixed exchange rate regime is due to be introduced in June to instil monetary discipline and restore confidence in the lev currency, which went into free fall in January while Bulgaria was without effective government.

Three smaller groups were set to enter parliament. The Union for National Salvation coalition grouping ethnic Turks and monarchist organisations seeking the return of exiled King Simeon had 7.8 percent so far, comfortably above the four percent threshold.
They are joined by the Euroleft, a new movement set up by Socialist dissidents, with 5.5 percent, and the Bulgarian Business Bloc, led by maverick populist George Ganchev, with five percent.

An interim cabinet led by Sofia's popular UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski has run the country since February, winning pledges of $1.2 billion from international lenders and kicking off the reform process the new government must continue.
Sofianski has said he wants to complete his mandate as mayor, but is expected to return to national politics at a later date.

After communist leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, leading communists re-emerged as the Bulgarian Socialist Party and continued in government. The UDF won elections in 1991 but their coalition with the ethnic Turkish party collapsed after only 11 months.

This time, the UDF has a secure majority. In addition, the Euroleft has pledged its support for their programme, while the UNS favour a coalition and the Business Bloc say they back Stoyanov and Sofianski but will not support a Kostov cabinet.
